KP 1. Identifying the Multiplicity of a Root of a Polynomial
1.?
The root of the polynomial P(x)=(x−6)6(x−3)2(x−5)4 with multiplicity 6 is x=
6
.
E
Fri, Sep 18th @ 10:02 AM|Elapsed: 0:47Correct

The multiplicity of a root of a polynomial equals the exponent of its corresponding factor in the factorization of the polynomial.

Note that the polynomial P(x) is fully factored.

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

  • The factor (x−6) has an exponent of 6 in the factored form of P(x). So the root x=6 has multiplicity 6.

  • The factor (x−3) has an exponent of 2 in the factored form of P(x). So the root x=3 has multiplicity 2.

  • The factor (x−5) has an exponent of 4 in the factored form of P(x). So the root x=5 has multiplicity 4.

Therefore, the root with multiplicity 6 is x=6 only.

First, let's factor P(x):

P(x)=(x−3)6(x−2)8(x2−9)2=(x−3)6(x−2)8[(x−3)(x+3)]2=(x−3)6(x−2)8(x−3)2(x+3)2=(x−3)8(x−2)8(x+3)2.

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

  • The factor (x−3) has an exponent of 8 in the factored form of P(x). So the root x=3 has multiplicity 8.

  • The factor (x−2) has an exponent of 8 in the factored form of P(x). So the root x=2 has multiplicity 8.

  • The factor (x+3) has an exponent of 2 in the factored form of P(x). So the root x=−2 has multiplicity 2.

Therefore, in ascending order, the roots with multiplicity 8 are x=2 and x=3.

3.?

1

Fri, Sep 18th @ 3:29 PM|Elapsed: 2:53Correct

Since x=1 is a root of p(x), the factor theorem tells us that (x−1) is a factor of p(x).

Because (x−1) is a factor of p(x), we know that (x−1) divides p(x) with no remainder. So, to begin factoring p(x), we can divide it by (x−1) using synthetic division:

x3 x2 x1 x0
1 1 −7 14 −8
↓ 1 −6 8
1 −6 8 0

Therefore,

p(x)x−1=x2−6x+8,

which means

p(x)=(x−1)(x2−6x+8).

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

p(x)=(x−1)(x−2)(x−4).

The factor (x−1) has an exponent of 1 in the factored form of p(x). So the root x=1 has multiplicity 1.
